subject: economics
chapter_title: The Theory of the Firm under Perfect Competition

concepts.title: Perfect Competition and Price Taking
concepts.definition: A perfectly competitive market has very many buyers and sellers of an identical product, free entry and exit, and perfect information; these features force every participant to accept the going market price, since charging more loses all customers and offering less is unnecessary.
concepts.key_idea: Size alone confers no market power, so the firm's demand curve is a flat line at the ruling price.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec204.txt, section 4.1, defining features and price taking, pages 54-55
question_patterns: which four market conditions force every seller to become a price taker

what does perfect information of buyers imply for sellers

solution_steps.explain: Confirm large numbers of buyers and sellers, a homogeneous product, free entry and exit, and full information.
With identical goods and informed buyers, any price above the market price sells nothing, so the firm adopts the market price.
The firm can sell any quantity at the market price, so its demand curve is horizontal - perfectly elastic - at that height.

concepts.title: Revenue: Total, Average and Marginal under Price Taking
concepts.definition: A price-taking firm's total revenue is the market price times the quantity sold, which makes total revenue a straight line through the origin whose slope is the price; both average revenue and marginal revenue then equal the market price.
concepts.key_idea: Since every extra unit sells at the same market price, price, average revenue and marginal revenue coincide.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec204.txt, section 4.2, Table 4.1 and MR derivation, pages 55-56
question_patterns: why does the revenue earned by a price-taking firm trace a straight line through the origin

solution_steps.explain: Total revenue is the market price times the number of units sold.
Dividing total revenue by output gives average revenue equal to the price; the extra revenue from one more unit, marginal revenue, is also just the price.

concepts.title: Profit and its Computation
concepts.definition: Profit is what remains of total revenue after total cost of production is met, and the firm is assumed to choose the output that makes this residual as large as possible.
concepts.key_idea: Profit is revenue net of all costs, and maximising it is the firm's single objective.

concepts.title: Profit Maximisation: The Three Conditions
concepts.definition: A profit-maximising competitive firm produces where price equals marginal cost on a non-decreasing stretch of the marginal cost curve, and only if price covers average variable cost in the short run or average cost in the long run.
concepts.formula: profit_maximum where market_price = marginal_cost (rising) and price covers average cost
concepts.key_idea: Produce where the last unit just pays its way, on a rising marginal cost, provided the price clears the average cost floor.
question_patterns: state the conditions for profit maximisation by a competitive firm
why must marginal cost equal price at the profit-maximising output
why can the firm not maximise profit where marginal cost is falling
why must price cover average variable cost for short run production
what happens when marginal revenue exceeds marginal cost at some output
compare the shutdown price condition in the short run and the long run

solution_steps.explain: While marginal revenue tops marginal cost, expanding adds to profit; once below, contracting helps - so profit peaks where they meet, that is where price equals marginal cost.
On a falling marginal cost curve the equality point cannot be a maximum, since a smaller output would earn more; the crossing must lie on the rising stretch.
In the short run price must at least cover average variable cost, and in the long run average cost, or shutting down earns more.

concepts.title: Short Run Supply Curve of a Firm
concepts.definition: The firm's short run supply curve is the rising portion of its marginal cost curve starting at the minimum of average variable cost, together with zero output at every price below that minimum.
concepts.formula: short_run_supply = rising_smc from minimum_avc upward; zero_output below it
concepts.key_idea: Above the average variable cost floor the firm follows marginal cost; below it, it supplies nothing.
question_patterns: what is the shape of a firm's short run supply curve

solution_steps.action: Read the price against the AVC floor
solution_steps.explain: Compare the market price with the minimum of average variable cost.

solution_steps.action: If price clears the floor, follow marginal cost
solution_steps.explain: The profit-maximising output lies where price meets the rising marginal cost curve, and all three conditions hold there.
At prices under the minimum average variable cost the firm produces zero, so the supply curve jumps from the axis to the marginal cost curve at that floor.

concepts.title: Long Run Supply Curve, Shut Down Point and Break-even
concepts.definition: In the long run supply is the rising marginal cost curve from the minimum of long run average cost upward; the minimum average variable cost marks the short run shut down point, the minimum average cost the long run one, and the point where supply meets average cost is the break-even earning only normal profit.
concepts.formula: long_run_supply = rising_lrmc from minimum_lrac upward; break_even at supply meets average cost
concepts.key_idea: The firm exits below average cost in the long run, and exactly at the average cost minimum it earns only normal profit.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec204.txt, sections 4.4.2 to 4.4.4, figures 4.9 and 4.10, pages 61-62
question_patterns: describe the long run supply curve of a competitive firm

solution_steps.action: Read the price against the average cost floor
solution_steps.explain: In the long run even fixed costs vanish, so the viability floor is the minimum of long run average cost.
Above the floor the firm equates price with rising long run marginal cost; below it, output is zero - the long run shut down point sits at the average cost minimum.
Where the supply curve meets the average cost curve, revenue just covers all costs including normal profit, the opportunity reward of the entrepreneur.

concepts.title: Determinants of Supply: Technology, Input Prices and Unit Tax
concepts.definition: Anything that moves the marginal cost curve moves supply: technological progress lowers marginal cost and shifts supply right, costlier inputs raise it and shift supply left, and a per-unit tax lifts marginal cost by the tax amount, also shifting supply left.
concepts.key_idea: Supply rides on marginal cost, so cheaper production shifts it right and costlier production left.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec204.txt, sections 4.5.1 to 4.5.2 and unit tax box, figures 4.11 and 4.12, pages 62-64
question_patterns: how does technological progress move a firm's supply curve

which developments shift supply rightward and which leftward

solution_steps.explain: Innovation trims the inputs needed per unit, lowering marginal cost; dearer inputs or a unit tax of t per unit raise marginal cost by that margin.
Lower marginal cost shifts the supply curve rightward - more offered at each price; higher marginal cost shifts it leftward.
A tax of t per unit adds t to cost at every output, so each price now buys the output the firm formerly offered at a price t lower.

concepts.title: Market Supply by Horizontal Summation
concepts.definition: Market supply at any price is the total quantity offered by all firms at that price, built by adding the firms' supply curves sideways; below the lowest shut down price nobody produces, between shut down prices only low-cost firms produce, and above them all do.
concepts.key_idea: Add quantities firm by firm at each price, remembering that higher-cost firms join in only above their own floors.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec204.txt, section 4.6, figure 4.13 and two-firm example, pages 64-66
question_patterns: derive the market supply schedule from the supply schedules of two firms

solution_steps.explain: At each price, sum the quantities supplied by the individual firms to get market supply.

concepts.title: Price Elasticity of Supply
concepts.definition: Price elasticity of supply measures the responsiveness of quantity supplied to price, computed as the percentage change in quantity supplied over the percentage change in price; a vertical supply curve is perfectly inelastic, and for a straight-line supply curve elasticity is read from where its extension cuts the quantity axis.
concepts.key_idea: Supply elasticity is a pure responsiveness number: more than one when the line's extension meets the quantity axis negatively, one through the origin, less than one otherwise.
concepts.textbook_ref: leec204.txt, section 4.7, cricket ball example and figure 4.14, pages 66-67
question_patterns: compute the price elasticity of supply from old and new prices and quantities

solution_steps.explain: Scale the change in quantity supplied by the initial quantity times one hundred.
Scale the change in market price by the initial price times one hundred.
Dividing the quantity percentage by the price percentage gives the price elasticity of supply.

worked_examples.question: Using Price Elasticity of Supply, compute the result for change_in_quantity_supplied = 3, initial_quantity_supplied = 3, change_in_market_price = 3, initial_market_price = 2.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Percentage the quantity response: percentage_change_in_quantity_supplied = 100 * change_in_quantity_supplied / initial_quantity_supplied = 100.0 Step 2: Percentage the price change: percentage_change_in_market_price = 100 * change_in_market_price / initial_market_price = 150.0 Step 3: Ratio the two percentages: elasticity_of_supply = percentage_change_in_quantity_supplied / percentage_change_in_market_price = 0.666667 Final result: 0.666667

worked_examples.question: Using Price Elasticity of Supply, compute the result for change_in_quantity_supplied = 4, initial_quantity_supplied = 4, change_in_market_price = 4, initial_market_price = 3.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Percentage the quantity response: percentage_change_in_quantity_supplied = 100 * change_in_quantity_supplied / initial_quantity_supplied = 100.0 Step 2: Percentage the price change: percentage_change_in_market_price = 100 * change_in_market_price / initial_market_price = 133.333333 Step 3: Ratio the two percentages: elasticity_of_supply = percentage_change_in_quantity_supplied / percentage_change_in_market_price = 0.75 Final result: 0.75
